summary.text: 飞 is the simplified form of 飛. The traditional graph is a whole-graph picture interpreted as a bird in flight; 飞 commonly means “to fly.”

formation.text: The traditional graph 飛 is pictographic: its whole form is interpreted as a bird in flight with outspread wings. The curated seal-script-style image illustrates this interpretation, but is a modern redraw rather than an ancient artifact.

components.text: The whole historical graph is interpreted as a bird in flight. It is not an internal component of modern 飞.

history.text: The curated seal-script-style redraw shows 飛 with a central upright and spreading sides, illustrating the traditional bird-in-flight interpretation. It does not establish the exact form of a particular ancient inscription.

A study reports no oracle-bone form of 飛 and cites an Eastern Zhou form in the Qin Gong gui. Chu manuscript, seal-script, and 說文 forms are also displayed, but they do not establish a continuous dated sequence.
The 1956 simplification scheme lists 飞 as the simplified form of 飛; it does not explain when or how the reduced shape first arose.

uncertainties.text: The exact appearance and earliest attestation of 飛, a continuous chronology of its forms, and the earlier history of 飞’s reduced shape remain unresolved.

senses.text: 飛 is glossed as a bird in flight, and early literary examples use it for flying. The composition dates of those works and the earliest secure surviving written attestation are unresolved.
Rapid movement is recorded as a sense, but its chronology and whether it developed from “fly” are unresolved.
“High” or “elevated” is recorded as a sense; its chronology and relation to “fly” are unresolved.

limitations.text: Rapid movement, high, unexpected, and unfounded are recorded senses, but their chronology and semantic paths from “fly” are not established; they are not connected here as developments.

The evidence reports uses of 飛 for 非 and graphic or borrowing relations involving 蜚, but does not establish their earliest attestations, chronology, or sound comparisons. No borrowing mechanism is asserted here.

Pictograph of a flying bird.
鳥翥也。象形。凡飛之屬皆从飛。

Pictogram (象形): a bird flying upwards.
In its modern form, resembles a tasseled 升 (shēng).
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *mV-pjər (“to fly”). Cognate to Tibetan འཕུར ('phur) and Garo bila.
This term also greatly resembles to Proto-Mon-Khmer *par (“to fly”), from whence comes Old Mon ပဝ် (pɔ) and Proto-Vietic *pər (“to fly”) (whereas Vietnamese bay).
Related to Old Chinese 翂 (*pɯn, “appearance of birds flying slowly”) and Old Chinese 奮 (*pɯns, “spread wings and fly”).

evidence.source: Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica, Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The 飛 entry displays Chu manuscript forms, seal script, and the 說文 form, and describes the graph as resembling a bird with outspread wings in flight. Its displayed stages do not establish an oracle-bone form or a continuous dated sequence.
evidence.title: 漢字「飛」：字形演變

evidence.source: Gao (study hosted by CUHK Centre for Chinese Linguistics Research)
evidence.text: The study says 飛 has not been found in oracle-bone inscriptions and points to an Eastern Zhou form in the Qin Gong gui. It also discusses historical interchange between 羽 and 飛 as graphic elements in some graphs. This is evidence about forms in particular compound graphs, not evidence that 飛 itself has 羽 as a component.
evidence.title: 中國語文研究／第4期 (Gao article)

evidence.source: 漢典, quoting 說文解字 and 段玉裁注
evidence.text: The 說文 entry glosses 飛 as 鳥翥也 and classifies it as pictographic. The quoted commentary interprets its shape as a stretched neck and extended wings, and says 蜚 was sometimes borrowed for 飛. These are historical lexicographic assertions, not independent proof of the graph’s earliest form or referent.
evidence.title: 飛 fēi - 漢典

evidence.source: 漢典, citing the Book of Changes, Book of Songs, and later works
evidence.text: The entry cites 易·乾卦 飛龍在天 and 詩經·邶風 燕燕于飛 for flying, and later Tang poetry for meanings such as floating or moving through the air. It records early literary examples but does not date the original composition or establish when each semantic extension arose.
evidence.title: 飛 fēi - 漢典

evidence.text: The entry separately lists rapid movement, high or elevated, unexpected, and unfounded senses, and cites Han-period uses of 飛 for the graph’s use as a loan for 非 and an old graphic relation to 蜚. These entries document later usage claims; they do not demonstrate that those senses derive directly from the flying-bird meaning or date their semantic development.
evidence.title: 飛 fēi - 漢典

evidence.source: 漢典, pronunciation and rhyme data
evidence.text: Modern Mandarin fēi and Cantonese fei1 are listed alongside Middle Chinese 幫母微韻平聲, fanqie 甫微切, and Tang reading *biəi. These data concern 飛 itself. No phonetic component is proposed in the pictographic analysis, so a sound-component comparison is inapplicable.
evidence.title: 飛 fēi - 漢典

evidence.source: State Council of the People's Republic of China, as transcribed by Wikisource
evidence.text: The 1956 Hanzi simplification scheme lists 飞 as the simplified form of 飛. The decision says the first table was to be used nationwide from 1956-02-01; 飞 appears in the scheme’s second table, for which the decision describes trial publication and later staged implementation. The text supports adoption within the 1956 scheme, but not the claim that the reduced shape originated in that reform.
evidence.title: 汉字简化方案

evidence.text: The entry reports that 蜚 was formerly used for 飛, cites 史記·秦紀 蜚廉善走, and lists 飞 and several rare graphs as variants. It does not provide sufficient dated glyph comparisons to determine whether any listed form is an ancestor, a graphic variant, or a later borrowing in each context.
evidence.title: 飛 fēi - 漢典

evidence.text: Search results identify a dictionary entry for 飛 and cite Guangyun, Kangxi, Cihai, GSR, and Hanyu Da Zidian references. Opening the entry returned HTTP 403, so no claims from its inaccessible page are used here.

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No independently inspected oracle-bone corpus entry or dated image was available; the claim that 飛 is unattested on oracle bones comes from the cited scholarly study.

No visually inspected manuscript or bronze inscription image was obtained. The Sinica entry labels displayed periods and gives an interpretation, but its text view does not expose individual glyph forms or their dates.
A specific chronology for graphic changes between Eastern Zhou, Chu manuscript, seal, clerical, and modern traditional forms is not established by the inspected evidence.
The dossier's broad simplified-form statement is supported, but the precise pre-1956 history and origin of 飞's reduced graphic shape remain unresearched.
The quoted classical examples attest flying uses, but exact composition dates and the first secure surviving written attestations were not established.
The semantic links from flying to rapid movement, high, unexpected, unfounded, and degree-adverb uses are not demonstrated historically; dictionary glosses alone cannot establish their chronology.

The dictionary reports borrowing/graphic interchange involving 蜚 and use of 飛 for 非, but the consulted evidence does not establish each loan's earliest attestation, chronology, or whether it is a whole-graph loan rather than an orthographic variant in every cited context.

No sound component is independently identified for 飛. Dossier claims connecting 飛 to Proto-Sino-Tibetan or other language reconstructions were not verified against primary comparative sources, so they remain outside the supported findings.

No Xiaoxuetang candidate was selected because the inspected search interface did not provide a specific 飛 result with exact source label and direct glyph URL; a queried character alone is not evidence that any visually similar candidate represents 飛.
The direct Commons SVG URL could not be independently opened in the web tool, although the Commons file description page exposed the original-file link and stated the reuse terms.
The Commons seal-script image is an educational modern vector reconstruction; it does not establish the exact appearance of a particular excavated inscription or its date.
